Providing Therapy When MCOs Deny Reimbursements.

39% (n = 39) of the sampled clinical practitioners' caseload is made up of clients with managed care insurance, of whom nearly 30% (n =29) have been denied reimbursement at some time for ongoing therapy, of whom 42.1% (n =12) later reenter therapy, and of the 12 who reenter therapy, 83% (n =10) do so with an acute exacerbateion of their symptoms.
39% percent of the caseloads of sampled clinical social workers and psychologists are made up of managed care insured patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of managed care organizations' denial of reimbursement on the provision of ongoing therapy.
the effects of managed care on the practice of psychotherapy and the ethical and legal ramifications of managed care for private practitioners.
the ethical and legal implications of managed care organizations denying reimbursement for ongoing therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this study suggest that managed care organizations have a responsibility to provide ongoing therapy when it has been deemed necessary by the treating practitioner.
12% to 14% of the sampled private practitioners are treating clients whose ongoing therapy has been denied reimbursement by their managed care organizations.

13% of all the clients seen by the sampled private practitioners are managed care insured clients who have been previously denied reimbursement by their managed care organizations and who later return with acute exacerbations of symptoms and who are now being seen by the sampled therapists.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the majority of our respondents (60%) reported that managed care insurance clients make up 25% or less of their caseloads, while 40% of our respondents report that 26-75% of their caseload are made up of managed care clients.
we have found that a large number of private practitioners in the United States have clients who have been or are currently denied reimbursement for ongoing psychotherapy.
managed care organizations are denying reimbursement for ongoing therapy to a large percentage of the clients of private practitioners.
The main takeaway from our work is that

managed care companies are not always acting in the best interest of the patient, and that private practitioners need to be aware of the potential pitfalls of managed care companies denying coverage for ongoing therapy.
private practitioners need to be more vigilant in monitoring the reimbursement practices of the managed care organizations with which they contract.

private practitioners should be aware that managed care organizations may not reimburse clients for ongoing therapy and should be aware that these clients may later reenter treatment with an exacerbation of symptoms.
